parts.title: Sentence comprehension: Woodwork studio note
parts.instructions: Read the short email from a friend. Choose the best word for each gap (1-5).
parts.passage:
Hi Ingrid,

I wanted to tell you about the wooden bedside table I found at a street market last Sunday. Although the dark paint looked awful at first, I quickly got [1] in scraping off the old layers. Our neighbour Pete let me [2] his electric sander so the tabletop would feel smooth. Next Saturday I am planning to rub natural beeswax into the oak, [3] should protect it from water rings. You do not need any expensive tools to start upcycling because charity shops often [4] sturdy old chairs for very little money. Let me know if you want to drop [5] and see the finished table!

Best,
Noah

questions.explanation: 'Got interested in + -ing' is the natural collocation; 'keen' takes 'on' and 'excited' takes 'about'.
'Let me borrow his electric sander' means Pete allowed Noah to use it temporarily; 'lend' goes the opposite way and 'rent' involves paying.
'Which' introduces a non-defining relative clause after a comma, referring to rubbing natural beeswax into the oak.
'Sell sturdy old chairs for very little money' fits the price phrase; 'give' does not take 'for very little money' and 'pay' does not fit a shop.
'Drop by' is the phrasal verb meaning to make a short casual visit to someone's home.

parts.title: Text cohesion: Restoring a dining chair
parts.instructions: The first sentence of the text is in the right place. Put the five sentences (A-E) into the correct order (gaps 1-5) to make a clear story.
parts.passage: Last month, I bought a scratched wooden dining chair from a second-hand shop and carried it into my garden shed. [1] [2] [3] [4] [5]
sentences: After wiping away the fine dust with a damp cloth, I brushed on two thin coats of sage-green paint.
First, I tightened the loose screws under the seat so the frame no longer wobbled.
Finally, I screwed the cushioned pad back onto the frame and placed the chair beside my desk.
Next, I rubbed medium sandpaper along every leg and rail until the shiny old varnish disappeared.

'Next, I rubbed medium sandpaper' follows fixing the wobble and removes the old varnish before painting.

parts.title: Opinion matching: Upcycling old furniture
parts.instructions: Four people (A-D) give their opinions about restoring and upcycling old furniture. Match each statement (1-7) to the correct person. You can use each person more than once.

texts.title: Layla
texts.text: When I furnished my first rented flat, flat-pack chipboard shelves fell apart within a year. Now I hunt for solid pine chests at weekend markets because old timber lasts for decades. I never cover nice wood grain with bright paint, though — I prefer sanding away scratches and feeding the surface with clear wax. Even if a drawer sticks slightly, a solid piece has far more character than anything from a catalogue.

texts.title: Gavin
texts.text: People think furniture restoration is a quick Saturday afternoon job, yet stripping thick gloss paint off a staircase or a heavy wardrobe takes real patience. Whenever I rush a project or skip sanding between coats, the finish peels off within months. Watching step-by-step tutorials online taught me to work slowly, label every screw in a jar, and test stains on a hidden corner before touching the front.

texts.title: Amber
texts.text: For me, upcycling is mostly about keeping useful furniture out of rubbish skips while saving money for my family. Last spring we rescued a faded coffee table from a neighbour's driveway and turned it into a bright yellow hallway bench. My children helped choose the fabric for the cushions, so every room in our house tells a story rather than looking like a showroom.

texts.title: Samir
texts.text: I love visiting community woodwork workshops because you can borrow expensive clamps and sanders without cluttering up a small apartment. Before I joined a shared studio, sanding a bookshelf on my balcony annoyed the neighbours with noise and dust. Having a proper workbench and advice from experienced volunteers makes tricky repairs—like replacing a broken chair leg—feel completely manageable.

parts.title: Long text comprehension: Giving old furniture a second life
parts.instructions: Read the article about furniture restoration and upcycling. Match each paragraph (1-7) to the best heading (A-H). There is one extra heading that you do not need.

paragraphs.text: Walk past almost any city rubbish collection point on a Sunday evening and you are likely to see a solid oak bookcase or a slightly scratched dining table waiting for the lorry. Inexpensive flat-pack furniture has made it easy to replace a whole living room every few years, yet much of that new furniture is built from thin glued board that swells in damp air and cannot easily be repaired once a hinge pulls loose.

Historically, throwing away a broken chair was unthinkable for ordinary households. Before mass-produced plastic and glued boards arrived in the mid-twentieth century, skilled village carpenters built chests, benches, and cupboards using interlocking wooden joints rather than weak staples. Families passed sturdy pieces down through generations, calling in a local repairer whenever a cane seat wore thin or a table leg needed re-gluing.

In recent years, rising living costs and growing concern about waste have sparked a fresh wave of interest in both restoration and upcycling. While traditional restoration aims to return an antique piece to its original condition, upcycling takes a broader, more playful approach. A creative owner might turn an old wooden ladder into a bathroom towel rack or repaint a dull 1980s sideboard in deep forest green with brass handles.

Beginners who want to try upcycling at home often buy far too many expensive machines before finishing their first project. In reality, a successful makeover depends mainly on careful preparation with three basic items: medium sandpaper, sugar soap for cleaning grease, and a good primer. Skipping the cleaning stage is the most common mistake, because kitchen oil or old polish stops new paint from sticking properly.

Choosing the right finish also shapes how long a restored piece will survive daily family life. Water-based chalk paint dries quickly and requires little sanding, making it popular for picture frames and bedroom drawers, though it needs a protective coat of wax or matte varnish. For busy kitchen tables that face hot mugs and spilled juice, hard-wearing oil or polyurethane varnish offers far stronger protection.

Finding affordable pieces to rescue has become a weekend treasure hunt for many hobbyists. Charity furniture warehouses, estate sales, and local online swap groups regularly offer solid pine wardrobes or sturdy wooden chairs for less than the cost of a tin of paint. Smart buyers always check underneath drawers for woodworm holes and test whether joints feel firm before loading a piece into the car.

Beyond saving money and brightening a home, working with wood offers a quiet mental break from screens and office deadlines. Measuring a shelf, smoothing rough timber by hand, and watching dull varnish transform into a warm satin finish provides a clear sense of achievement. As community tool libraries and repair cafés expand across towns, more neighbours are discovering that fixing an old object feels far more satisfying than clicking 'buy now'.

headings: How older furniture was built to last for generations
Matching the right paint or varnish to everyday use
Why modern cheap furniture rarely survives long
Essential preparation steps before opening a paint tin
Where to source sturdy pieces and what to inspect
How museum conservators date seventeenth-century oak
The difference between traditional repair and creative reuse
Personal satisfaction and the growth of shared workshops

gaps.explanation: Paragraph 1 contrasts thrown-away solid wood furniture with modern flat-pack cheap glued board that swells and cannot be repaired.
Paragraph 2 explains how pre-1950s carpenters used interlocking joints so families could repair and pass furniture down through generations.
Paragraph 3 distinguishes traditional restoration (returning antiques to original condition) from creative upcycling (repurposing or repainting).
Paragraph 4 focuses on basic preparation—sandpaper, sugar soap, and primer—and warns against skipping cleaning before painting.
Paragraph 5 compares chalk paint with wax for drawers against tough oil or varnish for busy kitchen tables.
Paragraph 6 lists places to find affordable pieces (charity warehouses, estate sales, swap groups) and checks for woodworm and firm joints.
Paragraph 7 highlights the mental satisfaction of hand-finishing wood and the growth of community tool libraries and repair cafés.

parts.title: Monologue comprehension
parts.instructions: Listen to two speakers giving short talks: first a community centre coordinator about a local repair café (questions 1-2), then a furniture restorer about turning her hobby into a shop (questions 3-4). Choose the best answer for each question.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: First, you will hear Samir, a community centre coordinator, talking about starting a monthly furniture repair café.

turns.speaker: samir
turns.text: When we opened our monthly repair café in the community hall, I assumed volunteers would spend the whole morning fixing kitchen toasters and torn coats. In fact, people carried in far more wobbly dining chairs, broken bookshelves, and loose drawer handles than anything else. At first, our volunteers simply fixed each item while the owner waited with a cup of tea. After two months, though, we realised nobody was learning how to do simple repairs at home, and the same families kept returning with similar problems. So we changed our rule: now owners sit beside the volunteer, hold the clamp, and rub the sandpaper themselves while we guide them step by step. I expected a few busy visitors to complain about doing the work. What genuinely surprised me was how proud people looked carrying their chair out the door, and several former visitors even signed up as beginner volunteers the following month.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Now you will hear Ingrid, a furniture restorer, talking about opening her own small upcycling workshop and shop.

turns.speaker: ingrid
turns.text: Friends often tell me how peaceful it must be to spend every day painting vintage dressers and listening to the radio in a cosy studio. Believe me, the reality is much busier than that! Stripping and painting a wardrobe is actually the easiest part of my week. What nearly overwhelmed me during my first year was moving heavy pieces up narrow staircases, measuring van space, and storing twenty unfinished tables in a tiny back room while waiting for customers to collect them. Nobody thinks about storage and lifting when they admire a pretty painted cupboard on social media. Still, I love seeing old timber get a second home. If someone asks me for advice before turning upcycling into a business, I always say: do not rent a high-street shop straight away. Start by restoring three or four small pieces in a garage or shared studio, sell them locally, and check how much time each piece really takes before signing a lease.

parts.title: Personal experience and discussion
parts.instructions: You have 1 minute to prepare and 2 minutes to speak continuously. Answer all three questions in one organised talk.

topics.prompt:
Talk about a time when you fixed, improved, or reused an old object instead of throwing it away. Answer all three questions in one 2-minute talk:
1. Describe the old object and what you did to fix or improve it.
2. How did you feel when you saw the finished result?
3. Why do you think repairing and upcycling have become so popular in recent years?
